claims.text: The native iron oxide film on untreated Q235 steel acts as a protective barrier under ambient conditions.
Aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C transforms the native oxide film on Q235 steel and compromises its integrity.
Heating converts dense, adherent iron oxides on Q235 into porous, weakly adherent, or spalling phases.
Oxide-film transformation accelerates Q235 corrosion relative to steels protected by Cr-rich passive layers.
The native oxide on as-received Q235 consists primarily of Fe2O3 and Fe3O4.
The native oxide film on Q235 forms during production and storage.
Increased diffusion and reaction kinetics at high temperature promote degradation of the Q235 oxide film.
Loss of oxide density and adhesion causes spallation and increased mass loss.
A robust Cr-rich passive film provides corrosion protection in stainless and Fe-Cr steels.
316 stainless steel maintains a stable Cr-rich passive layer under the proposed Na2SO4/NaCl exposures at 700–900 °C.
At ambient conditions, Q235 will exhibit minimal mass change and retain an intact, adherent native oxide.
At 700–900 °C, Q235 will develop porous, loosely adherent, or spalled oxides.
At 700–900 °C, Q235 will undergo greater mass loss than 316 stainless steel under comparable salt exposure.
316 stainless steel is an appropriate reference because it forms a stable, protective Cr-rich passive film.
Pre-passivation or annealing of Q235 may prevent the proposed native-oxide degradation mechanism from applying.
A substantially different salt composition may change whether the proposed mechanism applies.
The exact phase-transformation pathway and critical degradation temperature for Q235 are uncertain.
A lack of statistically significant oxide transformation at high temperature, together with corrosion performance comparable to 316 stainless steel, would falsify the hypothesis.
